To build a better healthcare system, we must support patients, but also support the doctors |Image used for representational purpose only | Photo Credit: Getty Images
There was a time when a patient simply asked, “Doctor, what should I do?” Consultations today, however, , sound remarkably different. Patients enquire if they should get surgery or take medication? Would a second opinion be recommended? What about side effects?
Modern medicine has handed us something extraordinary: choice. But it comes with a psychological paradox. Choosing an option becomes harder when there are more options. This heavy burden of choice now sits on both sides of the desk.
Illness already brings fear, anxiety, and uncertainty. Stack endless choices on top of that: which specialist, which test, which path, and decision fatigue sets in. It isn’t helpless collapse when an overwhelmed patient finally says, “Just tell me what to do.” It is pure emotional exhaustion.
Many people endlessly search for the ‘perfect’ choice, hoping to eliminate risk entirely. When there is a difficult outcome regardless, counterfactual thinking takes over: Did I choose wrong? But a crucial truth gets lost here: a good decision can still have a bad outcome. Choices should be judged by the information available at the time, not by what happens down the road.
It is also important to consider what happens across the table. Modern healthcare asks doctors to be clinicians, risk managers, educators, and empathetic partners, often within a single 20-minute slot.
Doctors must navigate a delicate tightrope. Be too directive, and you strip the patient of autonomy. Offer every conceivable option without guidance, and you leave them abandoned in a maze. Add in the ‘second-opinion paradox’, where different clinicians legitimately weigh probabilities differently and doctors must explain not just the disease, but why medicine isn’t simple arithmetic.
Patients understandably crave certainty, but ethically, a doctor cannot promise it. Trust isn’t believing a physician knows the future; it’s knowing they will be honest about what is known, what is uncertain, and how to adapt if things change.
More information doesn’t automatically empower. Raw data without interpretation only breeds distress. True empowerment happens through shared decision-making, a genuine psychological partnership where clinical evidence meets a patient’s personal values and priorities.
Sometimes, the most relieving words a doctor can say are: “Let us go through this together.”
To build a better healthcare system, we must support patients, but also support the doctors. The emotional labour of medicine is invisible on a prescription, yet physicians regularly carry one patient’s fear straight into the next room while remaining clinically precise.
Empowerment doesn’t mean offering the maximum number of choices; it means offering the right options, clearly explained, with enough support to make uncertainty bearable. The best healthcare never asks one person to carry the weight alone—it builds a partnership strong enough to carry it together.
(Dr. Sushma Gopalan is lead consultant – child life services (psychology), Manipal Hospital Yelahanka, sushma.gopalan@manipalhospitals.com)
